newsitem.title: USA: Talk of EMU concessions opens door for dollar/mark.
newsitem.headline: Talk of EMU concessions opens door for dollar/mark.

text.p: Reports of a softening in Germany's aggressive stance on EMU criteria helped boost the dollar to four-week highs against the mark on Monday and rekindled talk that the rate could rise as high as 1.80 in the months ahead.
Comments from a weekend meeting of European Union finance ministers in Noordwijk, the Netherlands, paved the way for a stronger dollar, experts said on Monday.

"If an inclusive version of monetary union looks more and more likely and we don't get any signs of inflation in the U.S. economy, then I think we could exceed the 1.80 (dollar/mark) level," said John Rothfield, international economist at Nationsbanc-CRT.

The dollar leapt more than a pfenning, topping 1.71 marks for the first time since mid-March, after British newspapers reported German Finance Minister Theo Waigel had softened his stance on EMU budget criteria.
Waigel later denied he had eased his typically firm stance. Still, dollar bulls celebrated reports he said "I have never nailed myself to the cross of three percent."

EMU rules require nations to achieve budget deficits that do not exceed three percent of gross domestic product. Inclusion of peripheral European nations like Spain and Italy in the single currency group would presumably require a weakening of the traditionally strong mark, analysts said.
"Germany is beginning to realize that the European Parliament may vote in EMU entrants that haven't made the three-percent goal," said Rothfield.

"What seems to be helping the dollar the most is the idea the mark may be weighed down or softened by the inclusion of some of these other countries," said Michael Faust, global portfolio manager at Bailard Biehl and Kaiser in San Mateo, Calif.
Analysts contrasted the perceived passive stance of Germany with its previously staunch defense of the mark.

At the last Group of Seven Finance ministers meeting in Berlin on February 8, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said "the dollar correction process ought to end about now." The greenback was trading at 1.66 marks at the time.
Bundesbank officials have been conspicuously silent in recent weeks as the dollar has crept back toward a three-year high against the mark, touched on March 7.
"Essentially, the German politicians and the Bundesbank appear to be standing aside. They don't really care where the dollar goes," said Richard Gilhooly, bond strategist at Paribas Capital Markets.
"If that's the case, the dollar just keeps rallying until such time as they actually voice some concerns," he added.

Though Tietmeyer denied any German capitulation over EMU rules, the Bundesbank's tacit approval of the dollar's continuing gains casts doubts on its pan-European successor's will to preserve a strong European currency.

"It's difficult to see how the new European central bank can start off with the same credibility as the Bundesbank because the Bundesbank has been sacrificing its credibility through depreciating the deutschemark," Gilhooly said.
In addition, the European central bank will face a daunting task in governing the economies of up to a dozen nations with widely varying needs, analysts said.

"The currency markets are very skeptical about the European Central Bank's ability to operate as early as January 1999 making monetary policy decisions over such a diverse group of countries," said Rothfield.
"We were already bullish on the dollar. This is another reason to be bullish," he added.
But dollar/mark's renewed ascent will likely face more fits and stalls in the months to come than during a 12-percent rally earlier this year, analysts said.
"The pendulum seems to go from (EMU) pessimism to optimism fairly quickly," said Faust. "I don't see this as being necessarily a smooth ride."

A telling interpretation of the weekend EU meeting came from European monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy, who said the confab confirmed the political will to meet the calendar and conditions for EMU.
Financial markets appeared to read such assertions as a thinly-veiled acknowledgement that the EMU train will arrive on time in 1999, regardless of the economic realities.

"The Waigel remarks have underscored the political commitment to the process," said Faust. "Though you may have doubts on their ability to make it, basically they're saying: where there's a will, there's a way."
